batch_name: Three Key Texts from the Ripley Corpus
description: Three historically significant texts attributed to George Ripley (d. ca. 1490) not previously in the database: the Cantilena (CRC 6), a Latin allegorical poem on the regeneration of gold; the Concordantia Guidonis et Raimondi (CRC 10), Ripley's doctrinal synthesis reconciling his two main alchemical authorities on the question of fermentation; and the Epistle to Edward IV (CRC 13), a Middle English poem accompanying the Compound. Primary source: Jennifer M. Rampling, 'The Catalogue of the Ripley Corpus: Alchemical Writings Attributed to George Ripley (d. ca. 1490),' Ambix 57:2 (2010) pp.125-201.

texts.title: Cantilena (George Ripley)
texts.analysis_html:
The Cantilena (also known as the Carmen perpulchrum totum opus enucleans, 'Very Beautiful Song Setting Forth the Entire Work,' and De lapide philosophico seu de phoenice, 'On the Philosopher's Stone, or the Phoenix') is a late fifteenth-century Latin allegorical poem in thirty-eight stanzas attributed to George Ripley, Canon of Bridlington (d. ca. 1490). Jennifer M. Rampling, in her foundational 'Catalogue of the Ripley Corpus' (Ambix 57:2, 2010), describes the Cantilena as 'one of the most artistically accomplished works in the corpus.' The poem survives in two textual redactions: Type I, associated with Giles Du Wes (Aegidius de Vadis, d. 1535), French-born librarian to Henry VII and Henry VIII, who transcribed the poem twice in the early sixteenth century and who may have been an original transmitter of Ripley's Latin texts; and Type II, which was printed by Ludwig Combach in the Opera Omnia Chemica (Kassel, 1649). The poem was also translated into English in at least four versions during the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and into German by Georg von Welling in his Opus Mago-Cabbalisticum (1735).

The Cantilena allegorises the alchemical process as a narrative of filial regeneration: a king (gold) regresses to the body of his mother (the prima materia or philosophical mercury) and is reborn in perfected form. The quintessence appears as a crowned maiden within the wheel of the four elements who drinks the blood of the 'Green Lion' (a Deckname for the sericonian starting material) and, in return, feeds it with her milk — an allegory of the circulation of the 'Lion' with the quintessence of wine. The underlying alchemy is closely compatible with the doctrines of Ripley's Medulla Alchimiae (1476) and Compound of Alchymy (1471), describing the preparation of the sericonian vegetable stone through the interaction of philosophical mercury with the imperfect metallic body. The phoenix symbolism (from the alternative title) reinforces the theme of death and regeneration that runs through the colour-stage framework of the magnum opus, since the phoenix dies in fire and rises reborn, just as the alchemical king undergoes nigredo before achieving the rubedo of the Philosopher's Stone. One of the two earliest copies of the Type I Cantilena, Cambridge, Trinity College MS O.2.16, was owned by Thomas Charnock (1526?–1581), who added English annotations; another (Trinity College MS O.8.5) was owned by John Dee.

texts.title: Concordantia Guidonis et Raimondi (Ripley)
texts.analysis_html:
The Concordantia Guidonis et Raimondi (Concordance between Guido and Raymond) is a short Latin prose treatise attributed to George Ripley, Canon of Bridlington (d. ca. 1490), which attempts to reconcile the conflicting positions of his two primary authorities — the pseudo-Lullian Testamentum (attributed to Ramon Lull) and the Scala philosophorum of Guido de Montanor — on the crucial question of the alchemical ferment: whether gold or silver must be added to the philosopher's stone as a 'ferment' to allow it to transmute other metals. Jennifer M. Rampling, in her 'Catalogue of the Ripley Corpus' (Ambix 57:2, 2010), describes this text as 'highly compatible' in alchemical contents with the Medulla Alchimiae (CRC 16, 1476) and notes that one Latin version (Type I) was included in the Bosome Book (CRC 3), suggesting a possible fifteenth-century dating; however, no surviving copy is earlier than the mid-sixteenth century.

The doctrinal problem that the Concordantia addresses was of central importance to Ripley's alchemical philosophy: the pseudo-Lullian texts (including the Testamentum) required that a noble metal (gold or silver) be added as a ferment to complete the stone; but the Scala philosophorum of Guido implied that the stone could be completed without such a ferment, from the philosophical mercury alone. Rampling's analysis in 'Establishing the Canon' (Ambix 55:3, 2008) shows that Ripley ultimately followed the pseudo-Lullian position on fermentation while adopting Guido's twelve-step structural framework for the Compound — and that the Concordantia represents Ripley's theoretical justification for this selective synthesis. The text opens with the statement: 'Forasmuch as Raymond speaking of the ferment of the stone...' and closes with the attribution 'whose theorick this is' followed by the name George Ripley, making it unusual among Ripleian texts in carrying an explicit self-attribution in the manuscript tradition. The Concordantia circulated mainly in an English translation but was later translated back into Latin (Type II) and was printed by Ludwig Combach in the Opera Omnia Chemica (Kassel, 1649); the German translation by Cardilucius appeared in the Magnalia Medico-chymica continuata (1680).

texts.title: Epistle to Edward IV (George Ripley)
texts.analysis_html:
The Epistle to Edward IV (also known as 'A Compend upon the Philosophers' Stone sent unto King Edward the Fourth') is a fifteenth-century Middle English poem in thirty stanzas, addressed to Edward IV (r. 1461–1483) and attributed to George Ripley, Canon of Bridlington (d. ca. 1490). Jennifer M. Rampling, in the 'Catalogue of the Ripley Corpus' (Ambix 57:2, 2010), notes that although the poem is 'conventionally associated with the Compound of Alchemy (CRC 9) as a dedicatory poem, the two works are not linked in the manuscript record until the second half of the sixteenth century.' The poem employs language similar to that of the 'Wheel' section attached to the Compound, and it refers to the author's studies in Louvain — one of the few autobiographical details in Ripley's works. An early dating is confirmed by the poem's presence in the 'Corthop Group' (MS Sloane 3579 and Ashmole 759, ca. 1475–1500), the earliest surviving manuscripts of the Ripley corpus, although the Corthop copies begin only at stanza 10 ('As the philosopher'), omitting the first nine stanzas addressing the king directly. The full poem opens: 'O Honorable Lord and most victorious Knight ... As the Philosopher in the book of Meteors doth write.'

The Epistle is significant as a record of Ripley's self-presentation to royal patronage: it frames the alchemical work as a gift to the king and rehearses the key doctrines of the Compound in condensed form. The poem was first printed in Ralph Rabbards's edition of the Compound of Alchymy (London, 1591), where it appears as a prefatory piece; it was reprinted by Elias Ashmole in the Theatrum Chemicum Britannicum (London, 1652), and a Latin translation appeared in Combach's Opera Omnia Chemica (Kassel, 1649), with a German version in the Magnalia Medico-chymica continuata (1680). The earliest copies in the Corthop Group are unattributed, a pattern consistent with the manuscript transmission of other Ripleian texts, in which the canon's name was attached to works originally circulated anonymously. The Epistle's reference to 'the book of Meteors' (Aristotle's Meteorologica, the standard Aristotelian foundation for alchemical theory) as authoritative confirms Ripley's grounding in the scholastic natural-philosophical tradition within which English alchemy developed in the fifteenth century.
